reference.source: Clinical genetics and paediatric nephrology references
clinicalPearls: X-linked dominant ciliopathy caused by variants in OFD1 on the X chromosome, encoding a centrosome and basal body protein essential for primary cilium assembly; it is typically lethal in hemizygous males, so affected individuals are almost all female.
Defined by the triad of oral, facial and digital anomalies.
Oral features include a lobulated or bifid tongue, tongue hamartomas, multiple hyperplastic oral frenula, cleft palate and dental anomalies.
Facial features include hypertelorism, a broad or flat nasal bridge, frontal bossing and facial milia in infancy.
Digital anomalies include brachydactyly, syndactyly, clinodactyly and pre-axial or post-axial polydactyly.
Central nervous system involvement may include agenesis of the corpus callosum, cerebellar and posterior fossa anomalies, intracerebral cysts and variable intellectual disability.
Adult-onset polycystic kidney disease is an important late manifestation that requires lifelong renal surveillance.
Allelic OFD1 variants can cause distinct disorders in males, such as Joubert syndrome, Simpson-Golabi-Behmel type 2 and X-linked retinitis pigmentosa.
reference.pathophysiology: OFD1 is located on the X chromosome and encodes a protein that localises to centrosomes and the basal bodies of primary cilia, where it controls centriole length and is required for ciliogenesis and left-right axis determination; oral-facial-digital syndrome type 1 is therefore a ciliopathy. Loss-of-function variants disrupt assembly of the primary cilium and impair ciliary signalling pathways, including sonic hedgehog signalling, which are essential during morphogenesis of the oral structures, limbs, brain and kidney. The condition is inherited in an X-linked dominant manner with lethality in hemizygous males, usually as early pregnancy loss, so nearly all surviving affected individuals are female; skewed X-inactivation contributes to the wide variability in phenotype among females. Renal involvement reflects the same ciliary defect in tubular epithelium and characteristically emerges as adult-onset polycystic kidney disease, distinguishing the renal course from the early structural anomalies seen elsewhere.
additionalDifferentials: Other oral-facial-digital syndromes (for example Mohr syndrome / OFD type 2 and further subtypes)
Joubert syndrome and related molar-tooth disorders
additionalInvestigations: Molecular genetic testing of OFD1, with attention to X-inactivation patterns in females
Brain MRI for corpus callosum, cerebellar and posterior fossa anomalies and intracerebral cysts
Renal ultrasound with longitudinal surveillance for cyst development
Hand and skeletal radiographs to characterise the digital anomalies
Detailed oral, dental and craniofacial assessment
Family pedigree including a history of recurrent male pregnancy loss
redFlags: Recurrent early male pregnancy loss within the family
Development of polycystic kidneys with declining kidney function over time
Structural brain anomalies with hydrocephalus or seizures
Feeding or airway compromise from severe oral or craniofacial anomalies
reference.prognosis: The outlook depends chiefly on the severity of central nervous system and renal involvement. Many affected females survive into adulthood but remain at risk of progressive polycystic kidney disease and kidney failure, so lifelong renal monitoring is warranted.
pitfalls: Treating an isolated cleft palate, oral frenula or a lobulated tongue without recognising the wider syndrome
Failing to institute long-term renal surveillance because kidney cysts appear later in life
Not appreciating the X-linked dominant, male-lethal inheritance during genetic counselling
Overlooking subtle facial milia and frenular anomalies as diagnostic clues
